---
title: "Reinforcement learning under partial observability"
description: "Perceptual representations, memory, and attention in partially observable Markov decision processes."
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- In a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), an agent must choose actions without directly observing the full state. Past observations can matter even when the current input looks the same.
- Learning what an encoder retains and learning how often its outputs occur are different problems. The projects below study each in turn.
:::

## From observations to actions

A policy seeks to maximize expected cumulative reward. In a POMDP it receives
an observation $x_t$ generated from the hidden state $s_t$. Its action $a_t$
affects the next state and hence what it can observe next. For example, looking
away from an object removes it from view without necessarily removing it from
the scene.

In the models considered here, an encoder $F(z_t\mid x_t)$ represents the
current observation, and a memory $h_t$ summarizes earlier experience. A policy
chooses an action from $(z_t,h_t)$: it might look back toward the remembered
object even though the current view gives no indication of its location. This
internal state need not retain everything needed for an optimal decision.

## Research questions

- [Learning informative perceptual representations](perceptual-representations.qmd):
  which distinctions should the encoder preserve? Predictive learning and
  reconstruction offer different training signals; neither by itself establishes
  that the result supports good decisions.
- [Computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd): given a
  useful encoder, can learning the distribution of its outputs reduce coding
  cost? The model asks whether progress in learning that prior rewards attention.
